coverage.note: Gaps found: no reversal path for late approvals, no late or missing settlement file handling, missing state transitions, missing go-live gates, and no HSM degradation path. The backlog (Section 25) and readiness table (Section 27) were checked before raising them.

Requirements, principles, decisions, flows and numbers were cross-checked across Sections 2-28. Contradictions found in idempotency scoping, CDE scope, RPO, the latency budget, the reconciliation timeline, the phase plan and network-token readiness. Ledger arithmetic and the latency sum (1,338 ms, 238 ms overhead) are internally correct.

Each Section 26 criterion was checked against its requirement. The FR-2, FR-5, FR-8 and NFR-1 criteria cannot demonstrate their requirements as written, and the NFR-2 and NFR-4 criteria will fail by design. The other criteria (FR-3, FR-4, FR-10 to FR-17, NFR-3, NFR-5 to NFR-7, NFR-9 to NFR-12) are adequate.

recommendation.issue: The fast-path key and lookup do not apply the (merchant, key) scope or the request-hash comparison that the durable path applies.
recommendation.rationale: P3 and FR-5 require scoping by merchant and rejection of a reused key with a different body. The fast path as written does neither.
recommendation.verification: FR-5 test: two merchants send the same key and get independent payments; a same-merchant changed body returns 422 while the fast-path entry is still warm.

findings.statement: Section 9.2 keys the Redis fast path as idem:resp:{idempotency_key} and returns the stored response on a hit 'without touching DynamoDB'. This contradicts P3, which scopes idempotency to (merchant, key), and FR-5, which requires HTTP 422 for a reused key with a different body. Section 9.1 accepts merchant order and invoice numbers as keys, so collisions between merchants are likely. A collision would return one merchant's payment object to another merchant (a data exposure) and silently skip a payment that was never processed. A same-merchant reuse with a different body would get the old response instead of a 422.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path is not merchant-scoped and bypasses the body-hash check

recommendation.rationale: Leaving an approved authorization unreversed ties up customer funds and contradicts P1 (the payment record as the single truth).

findings.statement: Section 11.1 classes 'no response within 2,500 ms' as retryable, and Section 11.2 discards late responses. Yet Section 11.2 says cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the previous attempt 'did not succeed'. A timed-out attempt may still have been approved by the first acquirer, and the second acquirer may then approve too, leaving two holds on the customer's card. The design has no path to reverse or void an orphaned late approval, which conflicts with P1 and with the intent of FR-5 and FR-7.
findings.title: Cascade after a timeout can produce duplicate authorizations; the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' claim is unsupported
